As a result extends up to 20 km from the surface, Oxygen, and Nitrogen up to 100 km, Hydrogen up to 125 km and other gases rise far above 125 km except Ozone. The atmosphere is made up of diﬀ erent layers of gases of diﬀ erent densities and temperatures. Based on the above factors diﬀ erent layers of the atmosphere are as follows- (1) Troposphere – The lowest layer of the atmosphere is called Troposphere. All the weather activities like clouds, hail, fog, blights, thunder, wind storm, etc are conﬁ ned to the troposphere. The most important characteristic of the troposphere is that there is a decrease of 6.5o C with an increase of every 1000 mt in altitude. This decrease of temperature with increase in altitude is known as normal lapse rate. The upper boundary of the troposphere is called Tropopause. (2) Stratosphere – Stratosphere (15-50 km) is the second important layer of the atmosphere. It lies between Mesosphere (above) and Troposphere (below). This layer of atmosphere is very dry in nature and has the least amount of water vapour in it. As a result, there is no weather activity in stratosphere. The stratosphere is used for aviation purposes as the absence of weather activities makes this layer ideal for ﬂ ying. Ozone layer is found in this sphere. (3) Mesosphere – This layer is found at an altitude of 50 to 80 km. The upper ceiling of Mesosphere is called Mesopause. (4) Ionosphere – It is an electrically conducting layer, which makes short-wave radio transmission possible over long distances. Ionosphere extends from 80 to 640 km. *The unique feature of Ionosphere is the phenomena of Aurora Borealis in North Hemisphere and Aurora Australis in Southern Hemisphere. (5) Exosphere – It is the topmost layer of the atmosphere and is situated above the Ionosphere. This layer had no deﬁ ned boundary. The Communication satellites are positioned in the Exosphere. 1. Join−> https://t.me/thehindu000 World Geography General Studies CB–157 The Insolation *The only source of energy for the Earth’s atmosphere and its surface is the Sun. The outer layer of the Sun i.e. the Photosphere release energy at a constant rate. As a result, the per unit area of the Earth also receives constant solar energy. This phenomenon is known as solar constant. *Distribution of Solar Energy – Normally the solar energy received decreases from the equator towards Poles. However, there are Temporal Changes in the energy received in every latitude. Since the Sun’s position in comparison to that of Earth shifts Northwards and Southwards during Earth’s revolution the maximum solar energy received also shifts North and South of the equator in the same respect. 20o North Latitude receives the maximum solar energy and not the equator. *Regions where the Sun’s rays fall in a slanted manner receive less solar energy as compared to that region where Sun’s rays are falling vertically. *Albedo is the measure of how much light that hits a surface is reﬂ ected without being absorbed. Earth has an average albedo of 30-35% whereas the maximum albedo eﬀ ect is produced by surfaces concerned with glaciers and snow (75-95%). Deserts have an albedo of 20-30%, Paddy ﬁ elds 3-15% and Prairies 10-20%. *Water vapours are capable of absorbing the Infrared radiation waves and the outgoing long waves of the dispersed solar waves however, water vapours are transparent to the ultraviolet rays of the sun, hence are incapable to absorb them. * On clouded nights the amount of water vapours in the atmosphere is more as compared to a clear sky night. The outgoing long waves are absorbed by the water vapours present in the atmosphere. Hence, cloudy nights are warmer than clear sky nights. *Heat Budget-Energy Balance – the rays of the Sun enter the Earth’s atmosphere as short wave solar radiation and they escape the earth as long-wave terrestrial radiation. The balance between incoming solar radiation and outgoing terrestrial radiation is known as Heat Budget – Energy Balance. *Long-wave terrestrial radiation plays a major role in keeping the atmosphere warm. The atmosphere is warmed by the diﬀ erence in incoming solar radiation and outgoing terrestrial radiation. This warmth is captured by Gases like Carbon dioxide leading to Green House Eﬀ ect and Global Warming. 1. Assertion (A) : The atmosphere receives most of the heat only indirectly from the sun and directly from the earth’s surface. Reason (R) : The conversion from shortwave solar to long wave terrestrial energy takes place at the earth’s surface. Code: (a) Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A). (b) Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A). (c) (A) is true, but (R) is false. (d) (A) is false, but (R) is true. U.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 1997 Ans. (a) The principal source of atmospheric and Earth’s surface energy is the Sun. Insolation is the incoming solar Energy intercepted by the Earth. The energy radiated from the Sun is known as short-wave solar radiation whereas the energy radiated from Earth is known as long-wave radiation. The long-wave radiation is absorbed by the atmospheric gases particularly by carbon dioxide and the other green- house gases. Thus, the atmosphere is indirectly heated by the Earth’s radiation. Increasing concentration of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane increases the temperature of the lower atmosphere by restricting the outward passage of emitted radiation, resulting in global warming. 2. Normally, the temperature decreases with the increase in height from the Earth’s surface, because 1. The atmosphere can be heated upwards only from the Earth’s surface. 2. This is the reason why temperature decreases as height increases. At high altitude air density is less with little humidity. Hence, statement (1) and (3) are correct while (2) is wrong.
